note: Vol. I No. 25. The issue that places three buildings the reconstruction had no address for: the Baptist meeting house (by a cabinet maker three doors from it), Newberry & Dole's store (by a bakery a few doors north of it, on South Water Street), and P. Pruyne & Co.'s store between Clark and Dearborn. Its page 4 columns 1 and 2 are the two halves of one set of printed lines, so several claims here quote one half and name the other; the claims say which. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST in this issue.

claims.notes: THE BRIDGE ORDINANCE, AND IT IS THE BEST EVIDENCE IN THE CORPUS THAT THE TOWN'S BRIDGES WERE RIDDEN AND DRIVEN OVER. No person may ride or drive over ANY BRIDGE WITHIN THE LIMITS OF SAID TOWN faster than on a walk, on pain of five dollars, half to the informer and half to the Corporation. Three things follow that the reconstruction had to assume before: that the bridges carried MOUNTED AND WHEELED traffic and not only foot; that there was more than one of them inside the town limits in May 1834; and that they were structures the Trustees thought could be damaged or made dangerous by speed — which is a statement about how light they were. It sits directly beside the first issue's ordinance forbidding the removal of plank from either of the bridges (1833-11-26, claim c027) and beside T-0001's walkable bridges. THE TOWN'S OFFICERS ARE NAMED: T. J. V. Owen as President of the Board of Trustees and Isaac Harmon as Clerk — the first time either office is filled by name in this corpus, the ordinances of 4 December 1833 having been read (1834-01-07) without their signatures surviving. THIS IS THE FULLEST OF THREE READINGS IN THE MONTH: 1834-05-14 (page 3 column 2, lines 2625-2634, claim c001 there) and 1834-05-28 (page 3 column 5, lines 3681-3689) carry the same ordinance cut differently, and 'Hanwox' / 'Hanson' / 'Hammon' across the three is read as Harmon on the balance of the three plus the paper's other Harmons.

claims.notes: A DWELLING HOUSE, IDENTIFIED, WITH A DATE AND AN HOUR ON IT. The whole of a dead man's movable property is to be auctioned inside his own former house at ten in the morning on Thursday 5 June 1834 — which says the house existed, was standing empty, and was big enough to hold a public vendue. Barnardus H. Laughton is already in this corpus through the administration notice of 1834-05-07 (page 3 column 3), where Sophia Laughton takes out letters; the Laughtons' two houses on the Aux Plaines are the landmark an estray notice in the same month navigates by (1834-05-07, page 3 column 3, line 2846, 'ove Laughton's two [ho]uses'). NOTHING HERE PLACES THE HOUSE — 'the former dwelling house of the deceased' was an address in 1834 and is not one now, and this pass does not join it to the Aux Plaines houses, which the estray notice attributes to a Laughton without saying which.
